title: Clare of Assisi (1194–1253)
hookLine: she follows Francis into poverty and leads her sisters for forty years

cards: Palm Sunday night, in the hill town of Assisi. A young woman from a noble family waits until the house is asleep. Her family has marriage plans for her.
She has other plans. She slips out a side door, through the dark streets, down the hill, to a tiny chapel in the woods where a man named Francis and his barefoot brothers are waiting with torches.
There she takes off her fine clothes, puts on a rough tunic, and Francis cuts off her long hair. By morning her family is furious. They come to drag her home.

teach.b: Her name was Clare, from the Latin for bright, clear. Her relatives found her in a convent chapel and tried to pull her away. She held on to the altar cloth and showed them her cropped head, and they gave up.
Soon her younger sister Agnes ran away to join her too.
Francis gave them a home at San Damiano, a small, run-down church just outside town, and there Clare led a community of women, the Poor Ladies, for the rest of her life.
Other convents owned land, so the sisters were secure. Clare refused.
She fought popes, politely and for years, for what she called the privilege of poverty: the right to own nothing at all, and to trust God and the kindness of the town for bread.
Two days before she died, the pope finally approved the rule she had written for her sisters herself. And she wasn't grim about any of it. The people who knew her described her as joyful.
Poor and glad. Once, the story goes, soldiers came over the walls of San Damiano. Clare, sick in bed, had the Blessed Sacrament carried to the door and prayed before it, and the soldiers left.
Near the end, too ill to get to Mass, she said she could see and hear it on her wall.
That's why, in 1958, the Church made her the patron saint of television.
Her sisters, the Poor Clares, still pray in monasteries all over the world.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Clare on 11 August, and the Poor Clares, her sisters, live enclosed lives of prayer and poverty in monasteries worldwide.

o: bright or clear, the Latin behind Clare's name
holy, a name for women set apart for God
a nun's vow to own nothing at all, ever

games.q: what's inside her story — tap the pairs.

s: she came from a noble family in Assisi and chose poverty.
Clare's own rule for her sisters was approved by a pope
two days before she died, in 1253.
Clare is the patron saint of television
named in 1958, because she saw and heard Mass on her wall when too sick to go.

games.q: you're Clare. your furious relatives have found you in a chapel and are pulling you toward the door. what do you do?
o: hold on to the altar and show them your cut hair.
games.why: she clung to the altar cloth and showed them her shorn head. they gave up, and soon her sister ran away to join her.

practice: Think of one thing in your life that's gotten too full, a closet, a calendar, a phone's home screen, a habit of buying, and picture it with less: not empty, just lighter.
Clare wasn't trying to be miserable; she was trying to be free. If you pray, you can ask for the gladness she had.

wordCard.voice: clara. Latin for bright or clear, Clare's own name, who gave up everything to own nothing at all.

orig.note: Latin: bright, clear, shining. Clare's name.

carryVoice: Your line: poor and glad. She chose it, and fought popes to keep it. Until tomorrow.
